## Overview

The Assamese are a socio-ethnic linguistic identity associated with the Assamese language and concentrated in the Brahmaputra Valley of Assam, where they are native and constitute around 56% of the valley’s population. Assamese is an Indo-Aryan language and is the official language of Assam. The population of Assamese-speaking people in India was 15,311,351 according to the 2011 Census, including 15,097,257 residents of Assam. Assamese society developed through long interaction among Austroasiatic, Tibeto-Burman, Indo-Aryan and Tai populations. This produced a culturally heterogeneous tribal-caste continuum rather than a single ethnic origin. Its folk-culture significance lies in the interaction of language, agriculture, Vaishnavite institutions, seasonal festivals, textiles, bell-metal work, foodways, music and performance.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Muga** — Muga is a natural golden silk described as exclusive to Assam. It is one of the prominent Assamese silks and is used in silk garments.

**Pat** — Pat is a creamy-bright-silver colored silk. Rural households in the Brahmaputra Valley produce silk and silk garments with excellent embroidery designs.

**Eri** — Eri is another Assamese silk variety, used for manufacturing warm clothes for winter.

**Gamosa** — *Gamosa* is generally a white rectangular cloth with a primarily red border on three sides and red woven motifs on the fourth. It is used daily, in prayer halls, during Bihu, and in welcoming and honoring guests.

**Mekhela chador** — Mekhela chador is listed among the traditional clothes and fabrics of the Assamese.

**Riha** — Riha is listed among the traditional Assamese clothes and fabrics.

**Jaapi** — Jaapi is listed among the traditional Assamese clothes and fabrics.

**Tongali** — Tongali is a waistcloth made from or worn as a gamosa by a farmer.

**Motif vocabulary.** Assamese-lion, dragon, flying-lion; red woven motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The sources list Suriya, Pirawn, Gamusa, Jaapi, Mekhela chador, Riha and Tongali among traditional Assamese clothes and fabrics. The gamosa is generally white, with a primarily red border on three sides and red woven motifs on the fourth, although other colors are also used. It may be worn daily after bathing, used by a farmer as a waistcloth called *tongali* or as a loincloth called *suriya*, and wrapped around the head by a Bihu dancer with a fluffy knot. It is also hung around the neck at a prayer hall and is offered to guests together with tamul. Elders receive gamosas called *bihuwaan* during Bihu.

### Architecture

 They mention the namghar, or prayer hall, and the sattra, described as a Vaishnav hermitage, as important social and religious institutions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Bell metal and brass objects are prominent in Assamese material culture. The *Xorai* is a manufactured bell-metal object and a respected offering tray with a stand at the bottom; it may have a cover or no cover. It is used for tamul-pan offered to guests, for food and other items placed before an altar in a naam ghar, as a decorative symbol during Bihu dances, and as a gift to a person of honor. Traditional utilities and symbolic articles made from bell metal and brass are found in Assamese households. Hajo and Sarthebari are identified as important centers of bell-metal and brass crafts. Cane and bamboo craft supplies household utilities, weaving accessories, fishing accessories, furniture, musical instruments and building materials. The sources also mention pottery, terracotta work, woodcraft, iron craft, toy and mask making, boats and traditional building materials.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources mention jewelry making as an Assamese craft.

## Music & performance

Assamese music includes folk and modern genres whose artistic basis lies in the history, culture and ancient traditions of Assam. Indigenous ethnic music is described as having a descending scale and tunes structured in a pyramid, generally using a pentatonic scale. This distinguishes it from the mode-based or raga-based forms associated with the rest of India. The connoisseurs divide classical Assamese music into Borgeet and Ojapali. Sankardev and Madhavdev are named as composers of Borgeets.

The sources list devotional genres including Dihanaam, Harinaam and Hiranaam; indigenous traditional folk genres including Bihu, Bhawaiya and Oi Nitom; and popular genres including Goalpariya Lokogeet, Kamrupi Lokgeet, Ojapali and Tokari Geet. Named instruments include Banhi, Sifung, Bihu or Uja Dhul, Tokari, Dotara, Gogona, Khol, Mridongo, Nagara, Pepa, Taal, Xutuli, Doba, Xinga, Bor Tal, Bin, Paat, Toka, Kham, Muri, Pati Dhul, Joi Dhul, Bor Dhul, Dhepa Dhul, Kahlia, Bortaal, Huluxi and Hutuli. Bihu songs and Bihu dance are associated with Rongali Bihu. The sources name performers and contributors including Bishnuprasad Rabha, Bhupen Hazarika, Jyoti Prasad Agarwala, Khagen Mahanta, Madhavdeva, Pratima Baruah and Zubeen Garg.

## Dance & theatre

Bihu dance is associated with Rongali Bihu, the spring Bihu and the beginning of the sowing season. It is also connected with Bihu songs. The sources list Bohuwa dance as a festival of the Sonowal Kacharis of Assam. The Vaishnava movement contributed to performing arts, and Sankardev created Ankia Naat, described as a one-act play, while Borgeets formed part of the movement’s literary and musical production. The sources also mention toy and mask making concentrated in the Vaishnav Hermitage.

## Festivals & rituals

Bihu is a series of three prominent festivals marking the seasons and significant points in a cultivator’s yearly life. Rongali Bihu accompanies the coming of spring and the beginning of sowing. Kongali Bihu is associated with fields that are lush while barns are empty. Bhogali Bihu is a thanksgiving festival after the harvest, when the barns are full. These are also known as Bohag Bihu, Kati Bihu and Magh Bihu. The day before each Bihu is called *uruka*. The first day of Rongali Bihu is Goru Bihu, when cows are taken to rivers or ponds to be bathed with special care.

Bwisagu is a seasonal festival of the Bodo of Assam and means the start of the new year. Jonbeel Mela, or *Chunbîl Melâ*, is a three-day annual indigenous Tiwa Community fair held during the weekend of Magh Bihu at Dayang Belguri, at Joonbeel. Ali-Ai-Ligang is the spring festival of the Mising people of Assam; its name refers to root and seed, fruit, and sowing. Beshoma is a festival of Deshi people celebrating the sowing of crops and begins on the last day of Chaitra, continuing until the sixth of Baisakh. Bohuwa dance is identified as a festival of the Sonowal Kacharis.

## Foodways

Assamese cuisine combines cooking habits of the hills, where fermentation and drying are used for preservation, with the plains’ fresh vegetables, greens, fish and meat. Rice is the central ingredient. The cuisine uses few spices and is characterized by endemic fruits and vegetables that may be fresh, dried or fermented. Mustard oil is the preferred cooking oil, and bhuna is absent. Food is commonly served in bell-metal utensils made by the Mariya or Moria community.

A traditional meal begins with *khar*, a class of dishes named after the main ingredient. Another common preparation is *tenga*, a sour dish; traditionally khar and tenga were not eaten together in the same meal. Fish is widely eaten, especially freshwater fish such as borali, rou, cital, maagur, xingi, bhokua, xal and xoul. Mas tenga is a signature sour fish dish, prepared with souring agents such as tomatoes, kajinemu juice, thekera, Ou-tenga, teteli, kordoi tenga or tengamora. Other named preparations include Xôkôta, Naroxingho masor jul, Pura, Poita bhat, Pitika, Bor and Fritter.

Green leafy vegetables called *xaak* are important, and the sources state that one traditionally has 101 different xaak during Rongali Bihu. Pitha is a rice preparation made especially for occasions such as Bhogali Bihu; named varieties include Til Pitha, Ghila Pitha, Xutuli Pitha, Sunga Pitha and Kholasapori Pitha. Jolpan includes Bora saul, Komal Saul, Xandoh, Chira, Muri, Akhoi and Sunga saul. Tea, or *saah*, is an indispensable part of Assamese cuisine. Meals generally conclude with *tamul*, betel nut eaten with betel leaf, edible limestone and tobacco. Rice beers and liquors include zou, aapong, rohi, mod, chuje, nam-lao, haj, hor and photika.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources connect Assamese literary culture with the courts of Kamata and the Kachari kingdom in the fourteenth century. Hema Sarasvati composed Prahlāda Carita, and Madhava Kandali translated the Ramayana into Assamese as Saptakanda Ramayana in the court of Mahamanikya. The Assamese language article identifies the Charyapada as ninth-century Buddhist verses whose language has affinities with Assamese, Bengali, Maithili and Odia. The spirit of the Charyadas is said to survive in folk songs called Deh-Bicarar Git.

Sankardev’s Ekasarana Dharma produced translated works and new literary forms, including Borgeets and Ankia Naat, while Madhavdev and others continued these forms. Bhattadeva translated the Bhagavata Purana and Bhagavad Gita into Assamese prose. The Buranjis became standardized prose documents concerning diplomacy, administration and general history under the Ahom state. Traditional paintings and manuscripts include the Hastividyarnava, Chitra Bhagawata and Gita Govinda.

## Language & religion

Assamese, also known by the endonyms Asamiya and Oxomiya, is an Indo-Aryan language spoken mainly in Assam, where it is official. It has long served as a lingua franca in parts of Northeast India and was the court language of the Ahom kingdom from the seventeenth century. It developed from Middle Indo-Aryan Magadhi Prakrit and has been written in the Assamese script and the Bengali-Assamese script. Traditional Assamese script varieties included Bamuniya, Garhgaya and Kaitheli/Lakhari; manuscripts were also written on the bark of the saanchi tree. Assamese has regional dialect groups including Eastern, Central, Kamrupi and Goalpariya, as well as the Cachar dialect.

Assamese society includes caste Hindus, tribal communities and Assamese Muslims. Ekasarana Dharma, associated with Sankardev and Madhavdev, created networks of satras and namghars for worship, literary production, performance and community life. Hinduization, Vaishnavism and indigenous traditions coexisted in the historical formation of Assamese society.
